about.title: About TRIFAIR
about.body: Why this platform exists and how NGOs run it with artisans.
about.heading: About TRIFAIR
about.lead: TRIFAIR is an independent culture-first student prototype built for a college project to demonstrate how technology can empower indigenous craft communities.
about.pillar1Desc: Centuries-old tribal narratives, folk art techniques, and forest lore documented respectfully with community consent.
about.pillar2Desc: Physical QR tokens traced directly to verified artisans and ground NGO partners, replacing generic store claims.
about.pillar3Desc: Zero hidden markups. Every single rupee is itemized before purchase so artisans receive their full skilled labor wages.
about.disclaimerDesc: All artisan profiles, craft records, and products shown on TRIFAIR are invented sample entries for demonstration purposes only. No real payments or commercial transactions occur.

sources.title: Sources & References
sources.body: Where our heritage information, ethnographic records, and craft histories come from.
sources.lead: TRIFAIR draws from public tribal research archives, Geographical Indication registries, and non-profit craft documentation.
sources.archivesDesc: Documentation on Warli, Gond, Dokra, and Bodo cultural traditions adapted from accredited cultural institutions and academic publications.
sources.giDesc: GI registry details link to public notices maintained by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (India).
sources.disclaimerDesc: Individual artisan profiles and product codes in this prototype are entirely sample demo entries.

consent.title: Community Consent Policy
consent.body: Only artisans and communities who have given free, prior, and informed consent are shown.
consent.lead: We recognize that tribal art, symbols, and oral histories belong collectively to their indigenous communities.
consent.principle1Desc: Artisans and community elders have full autonomy over how their stories and traditional symbols are represented.
consent.principle2Desc: If consent status is marked 'pending' or 'withdrawn', the artisan and all associated crafts are automatically hidden from the public catalog.
consent.principle3Desc: This student prototype facilitates direct NGO-artisan relationships without middleman ownership of intellectual heritage.

privacy.title: Privacy Notice
privacy.body: How this demo handles data. It stores only your display settings on this device.
privacy.lead: TRIFAIR does not track users, set marketing cookies, or collect personal browsing data.
privacy.storageDesc: We store only your theme preference, light/dark mode, text size, high-contrast toggle, and language choice in your browser's localStorage.
privacy.noBackendDesc: There are no user accounts, password databases, or payment gateways. All demo operations occur client-side.
privacy.clearDesc: You can clear your display settings at any time by clearing your browser cache or resetting localStorage.

help.title: Help & Frequently Asked Questions
help.body: Answers to common questions about using TRIFAIR.
help.faq1Q: How do I verify a craft tag?
help.faq1A: Visit the Verify page and enter the alphanumeric code found on your craft item tag (e.g., TF-SAMPLE-101), or scan its QR code.
help.faq2Q: What does 'Traced to a verified artisan and NGO' mean?
help.faq2A: It means the craft has been documented and validated on-the-ground by our partner NGO, directly tracing the piece to the specific artisan and village.
help.faq3A: We use an open formula: total = materials + (hours × rate) + ngo + shipping + fee. Artisans receive 100% of their labor wages.
help.faq4Q: Can I buy real products here?
help.faq4A: No, TRIFAIR is an academic student prototype using sample data. No real financial transactions are processed.

methodology.title: Methodology & Architecture
methodology.body: How TRIFAIR structures pricing, verifies community provenance, and ensures informed consent.
methodology.pricingText: Prices are computed strictly through the single priceCalc algorithm in api.ts. Total = materials + (hours × rate) + ngo + shipping + platform_fee. Raw materials are classified separately and never called artisan income.
methodology.provenanceText: Each physical item is issued a unique QR token verified against partner NGO ground records. The verification states include VERIFIED, PENDING, REVOKED, and NOT FOUND. Verification explicitly states 'Traced to a verified artisan and NGO'.
methodology.consentText: No artisan or community record is published without explicit free, prior, and informed consent. Any record where consent is pending or withdrawn is excluded from public visibility.
methodology.dataText: The records shown here are sample entries for a student prototype. They should not be treated as verified testimony or as a substitute for community-approved documentation.

stories.warliStoryTitle: The Tarpa Dance and the Sacred Sun
stories.warliStoryText: In the quiet dusk of the village, the elder plays the Tarpa, a wind instrument carved from dried gourd. Dancers join hands in an unbroken spiral, moving around the sacred sun. The circle of hands represents the cycle of life, harvest, and the eternal bond of the community with nature.
stories.gondStoryTitle: The Sacred Mahua Tree and the Birds of the Forest
stories.gondStoryText: The Gond elders believe that every living being has a sacred spirit. In the deep forest, the Mahua tree blossoms under the stars, offering nectar to all creatures. The birds carry the songs of ancestors from branch to branch, painting the story of life in bright dots and lines.
stories.dokraStoryTitle: The Lost-Wax Flame and the Metal Spirits
stories.dokraStoryText: For four thousand years, the lost-wax technique has coaxed brass from raw clay moulds. The artisan coils delicate wax threads, praying to the forest spirits for a flawless pour. When the molten bronze breaks through the clay, ancient ancestors smile.
stories.bodoStoryTitle: The Loom of the River and the Geometric Agor
stories.bodoStoryText: From childhood, weavers watch the rivers flow and hills curve. In every thread of the loom, geometric motifs called Agor are woven. These patterns carry prayers for rain, plentiful rice harvest, and the enduring resilience of the weavers.
